title: EGBE BOBASEYE OKUNRIN (ASIWAJU)
text:
Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota is a traditional age-grade association, a form of socio-cultural grouping commonly found within Ijebu communities and other parts of Western Nigeria. Such groups play important roles in promoting communal unity, preserving cultural values, encouraging social responsibility, and contributing to the development of their communities.
The association comprises men within a defined age bracket, generally spanning about three years. As the name suggests, Bobaseye Okunrin is principally a male group made up of individuals who have attained a reasonable level of social standing, financial responsibility, maturity, and community relevance.
The group places strong emphasis on integrity, dignity, unity, responsibility, and respect for tradition. Its royal identity and outlook reflect its close association with the traditional institution of Imota. The association enjoys the endorsement of His Royal Majesty, Oba Mudashiru Ajibade Bakare Agoro, Olufoworesete II, the Ranodu of Imota.



HRM Oba Mudashiru Ajibade Bakare Agoro


Since 2024, Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota has actively participated in the annual Ayayo Day Celebration, where the group has continued to distinguish itself through organisation, unity, cultural display, and active community participation.
In recognition of leadership, experience, and community standing, the association appointed Aremo Tajudeen Adekoya, the Aremo Oyemade and Chairman of Admos Hotels and Suites, as its Baba Egbe.



Aremo Oyemade


The group is presently led by a team of committed officers, including Mr. Mobolaji Ogunbowale, Giwa Egbe; Mr. Yusuf Akintunde Azeez, Otun-Giwa Egbe; and Mr. Ayodele Gabriel, Akowe Egbe, alongside other dedicated members who contribute to the growth and smooth administration of the association.
One of the association’s important traditions is its monthly rotational hosting system, whereby members take turns to host the group. This arrangement promotes fellowship, strengthens relationships among members, and provides a regular platform for deliberation on matters affecting the association and the wider Imota community. The most recent edition was hosted by Otun-Giwa, Agba-Akin Yusuf Akintunde Azeez.
With the 2026 Ayayo Day Celebration just five days away, Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota is fully prepared to make another strong and memorable appearance at the event. The group remains determined to uphold its reputation for excellence, unity, cultural pride, and distinguished participation.
As Ayayo Day approaches, the association looks forward to once again celebrating the heritage, identity, culture, and collective spirit of Imota, while continuing to stand proudly among the leading socio-cultural groups contributing to the progress and preservation of the town’s traditions.

title: EGBE BOBASEYE OKUNRIN (ASIWAJU)

MEMBERS PROFILE

Ogunbowale Mobolaji
The Giwa and Baamofin Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Mobolaji K. Ogunbowale, MCArb, ACTI


Mobolaji Ogunbowale is a distinguished legal practitioner and a Barrister and Solicitor of the Supreme Court of Nigeria. He is the Founder and Principal Partner of M.O. Legal, a commercial and litigation law firm providing professional legal services across a broad range of practice areas.
An indigene of Imota, Lagos State, Mr. Ogunbowale obtained his Bachelor of Laws (LL.B. Hons.) from Lagos State University, Ojo, Lagos State. He subsequently attended the Nigerian Law School, Abuja, and was called to the Nigerian Bar in 2007.
He is a member of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) and the Nigerian Institute of Chartered Arbitrators (NICArb), and is also an Associate Member of the Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria (CITN).
Over the course of his legal career, Mr. Ogunbowale has developed considerable expertise in commercial and property litigation, debt recovery, corporate law, taxation law, labour and employment law, and arbitration.
Through his professional practice, he has continued to demonstrate a strong commitment to legal excellence, integrity, effective advocacy, and the delivery of practical solutions to complex legal and commercial matters.


Yusuf Akintunde Azeez
Otun-Giwa and Agba-Akin Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Yusuf Akintunde Azeez, ND, HND, B.Sc. (First Class), M.Sc., PhD (In View)


Akintunde is a First-Class graduate and accomplished Statistician with strong experience in pharmaceutical regulation, research, biostatistics, and data analytics. He holds an M.Sc. in Statistics (Biostatistics) from Bells University of Technology, Ota, and is currently pursuing a Ph.D. in Statistics.
His expertise includes electronic data capture, statistical analysis, data science, pharmacovigilance, predictive analytics, and data visualization, with proficiency in tools such as R, SPSS, and Minitab.
He currently serves as a Violation Monitoring Officer in the Intelligence, Monitoring and Risk Unit of NAFDAC, where he contributes to regulatory intelligence, surveillance, compliance monitoring, and risk management.
He is also the Founder and CEO of Adept Data Solution (ADS), providing statistical and data science solutions to researchers, businesses, government agencies, and development organisations.
Within the professional community, he serves as South-West Coordinator of the International Association for Statistical Computing (IASC) and Public Relations Officer of the Chartered Institute of Statisticians of Nigeria (CISON), Lagos State Chapter, promoting professional development, research collaboration, and data-driven decision-making.


Abass Ayodele Gabriel
Akowe and Babalaje Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Hon. Abass Ayodele Gabriel


Hon. Abass Ayodele Gabriel is a Higher National Diploma (HND) graduate of Lagos State Polytechnic. He is a resilient, dedicated, competent, energetic, and results-oriented professional with extensive experience gained from serving in several reputable multinational companies within the private sector. His commitment to excellence and strong work ethic have distinguished him throughout his career. A respected politician, Hon. Gabriel has earned recognition through his impactful contributions to grassroots governance and public service. His vast political experience and exemplary leadership led to his appointment as the Supervisory Councillor for Budget and Revenue in Imota Local Council Development Area (LCDA), a position he served with distinction from 2017 to 2021. In recognition of his outstanding performance, he was reappointed to the same office for a second term, serving from 2021 to 2025. He currently serves as the Special Adviser on Information and Communication Technology (ICT) to the Executive Chairman of Imota Local Council Development Area (LCDA), where he provides strategic guidance on digital transformation and technology-driven governance. Beyond public service, Hon. Gabriel is the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (MD/CEO) of Ibirorun Global Services Nigeria, demonstrating his entrepreneurial acumen and commitment to business development. He is also the Akowe and Babalaje of Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin Asiwaju Imota, where he continues to play a significant role in promoting unity, leadership, and community development.


BadejO Adejuwon Ogodo
Ashiwaju Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Badejo Adejuwon Ogbodo, B.Sc., MPA


Badejo Adejuwon Ogbodo is a political scientist and seasoned public service professional with over a decade of experience in tourism administration and public sector management. He joined the Lagos State Civil Service in 2010 and was deployed to the then Lagos State Ministry of Tourism and Intergovernmental Relations, now the Lagos State Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture. In 2011, he was appointed Personal Assistant to the then Honourable Commissioner for Tourism, Mr. Disun Holloway, where he contributed to the implementation of key initiatives that advanced the state’s tourism agenda. In recognition of his dedication, professionalism, and outstanding service, he was promoted to the position of Chief Tourism Officer in 2025, becoming the first public officer from the Ikorodu Division to attain this designation in the Lagos State Public Service. His career reflects a strong commitment to promoting tourism, preserving cultural heritage, and advancing excellence in public administration.


Alhaji Alimi Kabiru
Seriki Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Comrade (Alhaji) Alimi Kabiru Oluwatobi, B.Sc. (Accounting)


Comrade (Alhaji) Alimi Kabiru Oluwatobi is a dedicated public servant, labour leader, and entrepreneur with an unwavering commitment to service, leadership, and community development. He currently serves as a mid-level officer in the Lagos State Local Government Service Commission, having joined the public service in 2007. He began his career with Imota Local Council Development Area (LCDA) before being deployed to Ikosi-Isheri LCDA in Kosofe Local Government Area of Lagos State, where he has continued to distinguish himself through diligence, professionalism, and exemplary service. Driven by a passion for advocating for the welfare and rights of workers, Comrade Alimi became actively involved in trade union activities from the onset of his public service career. His dedication and commitment to the cause of workers earned him the confidence of his colleagues, culminating in his emergence as the Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Local Government Employees (NULGE) in his Local Government. Beyond public service, he is the Chief Executive Officer of Kaybee Global Standard Enterprises, a Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)-registered company with over two decades of experience in the construction industry. The firm specializes in building construction consultancy, project supervision, general contracting, the production of high-quality building blocks, and the supply of a wide range of building materials.
In addition to his expertise in construction, Comrade Alimi is actively involved in livestock production and supply, with specialization in cattle, rams, and goats, reflecting his entrepreneurial versatility and commitment to contributing to Nigeria’s agricultural sector. Outside his professional and business engagements, he enjoys meaningful conversations on personal development, leadership, and societal progress. He values strong relationships with family and friends and is passionate about initiatives that promote growth, unity, and community advancement.


Oyebanjo Salaudeen Oluwatosin
Bashorun Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



ESV. Oyebanjo Salaudeen Oluwatosin, M.Sc. (Urban Development), ANIVS, RSV, MNIM


ESV. Oyebanjo Salaudeen Oluwatosin is a registered Estate Surveyor and Valuer, Licensed Auctioneer, and an accomplished real estate professional with expertise in property valuation, land administration, and urban development. A native of Imota in the Ikorodu area of Lagos State, he holds a Master’s degree in Urban Development and is a member of several professional bodies, including the Nigerian Institution of Estate Surveyors and Valuers (NIESV) and the Nigerian Institute of Management (MNIM). Before joining the Lagos State Government in 2023 as a Senior Land Officer, he built a successful career in the private sector, providing consultancy services in estate surveying, valuation, and real estate practice. His professional experience spans property valuation, advisory services, and land management. Outside his professional responsibilities, ESV. Oyebanjo enjoys reading and participating in sporting activities. He is happily married and blessed with children.


Odusanya Ismail
Balogun Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Odusanya Ismail, FCA


Odusanya Ismail is a Chartered Accountant with over two decades of experience, holding professional certifications from both Nigeria and abroad alongside strong academic qualifications. His expertise spans the three core pillars of financial oversight; accounting, audit, and taxation, including independent financial statement reviews and risk-rated assessments across construction, oil and gas, and public-sector subject matter, as well as rules and regulatory standards compliance. This breadth, rather than narrow specialisation, defines his professional strength. Alongside his professional practice, Ismail is currently pursuing postgraduate studies with a focus on financial ethics — reinforcing a career-long conviction that sound financial stewardship is inseparable from questions of integrity and public accountability. In 2004, Ismail joined the Lagos State Local Government Civil Service Commission, where he was deployed to the Imota Local Council Development Area (LCDA). Since then, he has advanced steadily through the ranks to a higher cadre, a progression that reflects sustained competence, reliability, and institutional trust.


Chief Oguntola Abayomi
Otunba Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



OTUNBA ABAYOMI TAOVIC OGUNTOLA (Akindein of Imota)


The managing director/ Chief Executive Officer of DETITAAB MULTIBIZ SERVICES LIMITED. A Realtor with a vast knowledge in properties development/ Estate management, consultant in freight Logistics and also a consultant in conflict management. This Establishment has been in existence over a decade and its well manager under my supervision. A well-rooted society service provider through an international charity organization known as Lions club international (LCI). An officer of the Law with the rank of Assistant Superintendent of Police (SPY). Happily married with Children.


Oladega Musbau Lawrence
Tunwase Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Oladega Musbau Lawrence


Oladega M. Lawrence is an accomplished entrepreneur, project management professional, and real estate practitioner with extensive experience in business development, property investment, land documentation, and strategic partnerships.
He is the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Bauglobal Resources Ltd., a real estate company focused on land acquisition, property development, documentation, investment advisory, and innovative real estate solutions.


Bldr. Ayokanmi Oladunni
Maiyegun Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Bldr. Ayokanmi Oladunni (MNIOB, MNISP)


A Registered Builder and Safety Professional with well over two decades experience in Building and Civil Engineering Construction. Holds an HND in Building Technology, a PGD in Quantity Surveying, and an MSc in Construction Management. Founder of Work Ethics Nigeria Limited, a leading indigenous construction firm renowned for quality delivery, and excellence in project execution. With core expertise in Construction Project mgt, Resource allocation, and On-site supervision Beyond construction, he is a committed community support leader and holds a traditional chieftaincy title of Bashorun in recognition of his service and contributions to community development. Bashorun Ayokanmi Oladunni is fulfilled and happily married


Salisu Olugbenga Gabriel
Asoju Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Olugbenga Gabriel Salisu – Regional Branch Manager, Heirs/UBA


Olugbenga Gabriel Salisu is an accomplished financial services professional with over 20 years of experience in Nigeria’s financial industry. He has built a strong reputation for strategic leadership, operational excellence, and driving business growth across leading insurance and banking institutions. As Regional Branch Manager at Heirs/UBA, he leads branch performance, retail expansion, agent development, and customer-focused service delivery, contributing significantly to the company’s growth and market presence. Before joining Heirs/UBA, Olugbenga held senior roles at Leadway Assurance, AIICO Insurance Plc, Access Bank, and GTBank, where he successfully led sales strategies, managed high-performing teams, and expanded market reach across retail and corporate segments. Passionate about financial inclusion and customer empowerment, he is recognized for building high-performing teams, strengthening branch operations, and mentoring emerging professionals. His collaborative leadership style and commitment to excellence have earned him a reputation as a results-driven transformational leader.


Sigbeku Sesan Adebowale
Ashipa Egbe Bobaseye Okunrin (Asiwaju), Imota



Executive Director, Fimokins Global Concepts


Sesan Adebowale Sigbeku is a seasoned business executive with extensive experience in the commercial printing industry. As the Executive Director of Fimokins Global Concepts, he has successfully positioned the company as a trusted provider of high-quality printing and branding solutions. With expertise spanning large-format printing, corporate branding, packaging, and integrated print solutions, Sesan has built a reputation for delivering exceptional quality, precision, and customer-focused service. His strategic leadership, commitment to operational excellence, and strong client relationships have been instrumental in the company’s sustained growth and industry recognition. Driven by innovation and a passion for excellence, he is dedicated to helping businesses transform their brand identity into compelling visual experiences through world-class print solutions. His unwavering commitment to quality, reliability, and continuous improvement continues to set Fimokins Global Concepts apart in a highly competitive marketplace.

title: CISON 49TH Conference
text:
The 2nd CISON International Conference and 49th Annual Conference of the Chartered Institute of Statisticians of Nigeria (CISON) was successfully held from September 22 to September 26, 2025, at the Dome Event Centre, Asaba, Delta State.
The conference was preceded by a highly relevant pre-conference programme titled “Big Data Analytics and Machine Learning: Methods and Applications.” The session provided participants with practical and conceptual insights into contemporary analytical methods, machine-learning techniques, and their applications across research, public administration, business, regulation, and national development. It served as an appropriate foundation for the main conference discussions and reflected the growing importance of advanced analytics in modern statistical practice.
As both a participant and reporter at the conference, I found the gathering highly significant, intellectually stimulating, and professionally rewarding. It brought together statisticians, researchers, academics, policymakers, government officials, data professionals, students, and other stakeholders from across Nigeria and beyond to deliberate on the expanding role of data and analytics in national development.
The conference, themed “Big Data and Analytics in Nigeria: Developing a National Data Ecosystem for Enhanced National Prosperity,” provided a timely platform for discussing how Nigeria can strengthen its statistical and data infrastructure to support evidence-based policymaking, development planning, economic management, institutional effectiveness, and sustainable national prosperity.
A notable feature of the conference was the participation of a delegation from the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC). The Agency was represented by myself, Aare Yusuf Akintunde Azeez, from Lagos; Mrs. Alegbe; Mr. Felix Temange; Hajia Mariam; and Mr. Mujaya from Abuja. Our participation provided an opportunity to engage with emerging developments in statistics, data analytics, and machine learning, while also interacting with professionals from academia, government institutions, regulatory agencies, and the private sector. The conference was particularly relevant to NAFDAC’s increasing reliance on data-driven approaches to research, surveillance, regulatory intelligence, monitoring, and decision-making.



group photograph of participants at Asaba onference


The conference featured several activities beyond formal paper presentations and technical sessions. There were professional engagements, interactive discussions, networking sessions, knowledge-sharing opportunities, and social activities that enabled participants to reconnect, exchange ideas, and strengthen professional relationships. These activities contributed significantly to the success of the conference and created an atmosphere of intellectual engagement and professional fellowship.
The Lagos State Chapter of CISON was also prominently represented throughout the conference. Members actively participated in the various technical and social activities, reflecting the Chapter’s commitment to the advancement of the statistical profession. Several photographs were taken by members of the Lagos Chapter to document memorable moments, professional interactions, and the collective participation of members during the conference.
Another important aspect of the gathering was the presence of many distinguished professors, senior academics, researchers, and experienced practitioners from various universities and institutions. Their participation added considerable intellectual depth to the proceedings. The interaction between senior scholars and younger professionals provided opportunities for mentoring, knowledge exchange, collaboration, and exposure to emerging statistical ideas and research methodologies.
One of the strongest messages from the conference was that Nigeria’s development aspirations cannot be effectively achieved without credible, timely, accessible, and properly coordinated data. In an era in which data has become a strategic national resource, the quality of decisions made by governments, businesses, regulatory institutions, and development organisations increasingly depends on the quality and reliability of available information.
The Executive Governor of Delta State, Rt. Hon. Sheriff Oborevwori, as host of the conference, emphasised the importance of developing a robust national data infrastructure capable of supporting effective governance and national development. His message reinforced the need for governments at all levels to recognise statistics not merely as an administrative exercise but as a critical instrument for planning, resource allocation, performance measurement, accountability, and policy formulation.



LASUSTech staff and myself


The conference also featured important contributions from the President of the Chartered Institute of Statisticians of Nigeria, Dr. Ebuh Godday, who highlighted the professional responsibilities of statisticians in strengthening Nigeria’s evolving data ecosystem. His address underscored the importance of professional competence, ethical statistical practice, capacity development, and the greater utilisation of statistical evidence in both public and private sector decision-making.
Also prominent was the participation of the Statistician-General of the Federation, Prince Adeyemi Adeniran, whose presence further demonstrated the central role of official statistics in national planning and development. Contributions from representatives of institutions including the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Federal Ministry of Education broadened the discourse and demonstrated the relevance of data and analytics across virtually every sector of national life.



Myself and prof Kazeem Obisesan


Throughout the conference, discussions focused on the opportunities presented by big data, data analytics, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and modern statistical techniques, while also recognising significant challenges such as data fragmentation, inadequate infrastructure, capacity gaps, inconsistent data standards, limited institutional collaboration, and the need for stronger data governance frameworks.
As a practising Statistician, the conference was particularly enriching. It provided an opportunity not only to listen to leading professionals, professors, policymakers, and researchers, but also to interact with colleagues, exchange ideas, establish professional contacts, and reflect on the changing responsibilities of statisticians in an increasingly data-driven world.
One major takeaway for me was that the future of Statistics extends far beyond the traditional collection, tabulation, and presentation of figures. The modern Statistician must increasingly possess the capacity to transform large and complex datasets into actionable intelligence, identify patterns and risks, apply machine-learning and analytical techniques, communicate findings effectively, and provide evidence that can guide policy and strategic decisions.
The conference equally highlighted the need for stronger collaboration among the National Bureau of Statistics, government ministries and agencies, regulatory institutions, universities, research organisations, professional bodies, private-sector organisations, and technology companies. A functional national data ecosystem cannot thrive where institutions operate in isolation. Data must be integrated, harmonised, properly governed, and utilised in a manner that promotes quality, accessibility, security, interoperability, and responsible use.



Isah avery long time friend at Dome, Asaba


The five-day gathering in Asaba was therefore more than an annual professional conference. It represented an important national conversation about the future of Nigeria’s data architecture and the responsibility of statisticians in shaping that future. It was equally a celebration of professional fellowship, academic excellence, research, innovation, and the growing relevance of Statistics in national development.
For me as a participant and member of the NAFDAC delegation, the experience further strengthened my conviction that data must move from the background of institutional and national decision-making to the centre of policy, planning, regulation, and development. Nigeria possesses enormous volumes of administrative, economic, health, educational, regulatory, demographic, and commercial data. The major task before us is to transform these scattered data resources into reliable knowledge capable of improving governance, institutional performance, and the lives of citizens.
The 2nd CISON International Conference and 49th Annual Conference ultimately provided an excellent platform for professional networking, intellectual engagement, academic interaction, institutional collaboration, capacity development, and renewed advocacy for a stronger national statistical system.
As Nigeria advances further into the era of Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and digital transformation, the message from Asaba remains both timely and compelling: a nation that seeks sustainable prosperity must first understand itself through credible data.



At Dome, Asaba @ CISON Conference


The responsibility therefore rests on statisticians, researchers, academics, regulators, policymakers, and institutions to build a national data ecosystem in which evidence becomes the foundation of planning, regulation, innovation, and development rather than an afterthought.
Reported by:
Aare Yusuf Akintunde Azeez
Statistician | Data Analyst | Researcher
NAFDAC Representative and Participant
2nd CISON International Conference & 49th Annual Conference
Asaba, Delta State — September 2025

As Nigeria advances further into the era of Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and digital transformation, the message from Asaba remains both timely and compelling: a nation that seeks sustainable prosperity must first understand itself through credible data.



At Dome, Asaba @ CISON Conference


The responsibility therefore rests on statisticians, researchers, academics, regulators, policymakers, and institutions to build a national data ecosystem in which evidence becomes the foundation of planning, regulation, innovation, and development rather than an afterthought.

title: Yusuf Akintunde Azeez
text:
Yusuf Akintunde Azeez (Aare) is an accomplished Statistician, researcher, and public-sector professional with over twenty (20) years of experience in the analysis, interpretation, and application of complex data for planning, research, and decision-making. He possesses strong practical knowledge of statistical tools and methodologies, with proven competence in sampling, data validation, statistical modelling, research design, and the use of computer-based analytical applications.
He has a broad understanding of statistical concepts, methods, and models, complemented by strong commercial awareness, excellent presentation skills, effective verbal communication, and sound organisational ability. His professional interest is centred on research, data-driven decision-making, process improvement, and the continuous evaluation and recommendation of procedures that support institutional efficiency and the achievement of corporate objectives.
Aare Akintunde Yusuf began his professional development at the Nigerian Railway Traffic Training School, Enugu, where he obtained a Proficiency Certificate in Traffic and Commercial Operations of Railway Activities. He subsequently undertook a Professional Diploma in Statistics (PDS) at the University of Ibadan before proceeding to Kwara State Polytechnic, Ilorin, where he obtained both a National Diploma in Mathematics and Statistics and a Higher National Diploma in Statistics, graduating with Distinction.
In pursuit of further academic advancement, he proceeded to Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, for postgraduate studies in Statistics. He later obtained a Master’s degree in Statistics from Bells University of Technology, Ota, Ogun State. Demonstrating a strong commitment to continuous learning and academic excellence, and in response to the long-standing HND/B.Sc. dichotomy in Nigeria, he returned to university to earn a Bachelor of Science degree in Applied Mathematics from Bells University of Technology, graduating with First Class Honours.
Professionally, Aare is a member of the Chartered Institute of Statisticans of Nigeria (CISON) and currently serves as the South-West Coordinator of the International Association for Statistical Computing (IASC). He is also the Public Relations Officer of the Chartered Institute of Statisticians of Nigeria, Lagos State Chapter.
Beyond his professional and academic engagements, he is actively involved in community leadership and service. He is the current and Pioneer President of De Royal Ambassadors of Imota, and also holds the traditional/community titles of Agba-Akin and Otun-Giwa Bobaseye of Imota.
Aare Akintunde Yusuf’s profile reflects a combination of academic distinction, professional competence, leadership, and commitment to service. His journey demonstrates resilience, continuous self-development, and a firm belief in the power of statistics, research, and informed analysis to improve institutions and society.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
My journey into statistics, programming, data analysis, and data science has always been driven by one central goal: to move beyond merely understanding statistical concepts and become capable of applying them confidently using modern analytical tools.
As part of that journey, I undertook an intensive programming and data-analysis training programme with GBG Analytics, running from 21 July to 7 October 2026.
The training used a lab-based approach, with emphasis on practical learning, hands-on exercises, demonstrations, assignments, independent practice, and supporting video materials. This approach meant that the programme was not simply about watching someone write code or memorising R functions. I was required to write the code myself, work with datasets, make mistakes, troubleshoot errors, create visualisations, document my analysis, and gradually develop complete analytical projects.
That practical method made R considerably easier for me.



R language symbol


Before the training, R sometimes appeared to be a collection of unfamiliar functions, symbols, packages, brackets, and error messages. As the training progressed, however, I began to understand the logic behind the language and, more importantly, how the different components of the data-analysis process connect.
The programme covered Introduction to R Programming, data manipulation and cleaning, data visualisation with ggplot2 and Base R, data merging and joining, Markdown and reproducible reporting, Quarto publishing, and Git/GitHub.
What made the programme especially valuable was that these topics were not treated as isolated subjects. They gradually came together to form a complete workflow—from raw data to a finished analytical product published on the web.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
My journey into statistics, programming, data analysis, and data science has always been driven by one central goal: to move beyond merely understanding statistical concepts and become capable of applying them confidently using modern analytical tools.
As part of that journey, I undertook an intensive programming and data-analysis training programme with GBG Analytics, running from 21 July to 7 October 2026.
The training used a lab-based approach, with emphasis on practical learning, hands-on exercises, demonstrations, assignments, independent practice, and supporting video materials. This approach meant that the programme was not simply about watching someone write code or memorising R functions. I was required to write the code myself, work with datasets, make mistakes, troubleshoot errors, create visualisations, document my analysis, and gradually develop complete analytical projects.
That practical method made R considerably easier for me.



R language symbol


Before the training, R sometimes appeared to be a collection of unfamiliar functions, symbols, packages, brackets, and error messages. As the training progressed, however, I began to understand the logic behind the language and, more importantly, how the different components of the data-analysis process connect.
The programme covered Introduction to R Programming, data manipulation and cleaning, data visualisation with ggplot2 and Base R, data merging and joining, Markdown and reproducible reporting, Quarto publishing, and Git/GitHub.
What made the programme especially valuable was that these topics were not treated as isolated subjects. They gradually came together to form a complete workflow—from raw data to a finished analytical product published on the web.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Introduction to R Programming
The training began with the fundamentals of R programming.
This stage helped me understand how R stores and processes information and how analytical operations are built from relatively simple components.
I learnt how to create objects and assign values using expressions such as:

x <- 10

We explored major R data types, including numeric, integer, character, logical and factor variables, as well as important data structures such as vectors, matrices, lists, factors and data frames.
For example:

age <- c(25, 31, 28, 40, 36)

creates a numeric vector containing five observations.
I became familiar with fundamental functions such as mean() for arithmetic means, median() for the middle value, sum() for totals, min() and max() for extreme values, and sd() for standard deviation.
Functions such as summary(), str(), head(), tail(), table(), unique(), length() and is.na() became important tools for understanding and checking datasets.
The training helped me appreciate an important principle: before analysing data, the analyst must first understand the data.
Knowing how R represents numeric, categorical, logical, and missing information is fundamental because the structure and type of a variable determine which analytical techniques are appropriate.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Data Manipulation and Cleaning
The next important area was data manipulation and data cleaning.
Real-world data rarely arrive in a perfectly organised state. Data may contain missing observations, poorly labelled variables, duplicates, inconsistent categories, unnecessary columns, incorrect data types, or information that needs to be transformed before meaningful analysis can begin.
I therefore learnt to use the dplyr package extensively.
Functions such as select() allow an analyst to choose particular variables, while filter() makes it possible to retain observations satisfying specific conditions.
For example:

# data |>
#  filter(age >= 18)

can retain observations where age is at least 18.
I learnt to use arrange() for sorting data, mutate() for creating new variables, rename() for changing variable names, distinct() for dealing with unique records, and count() for obtaining category frequencies.
The combination of group_by() and summarise() was particularly useful because it allowed me to calculate statistics separately for meaningful groups.
For example:
data |>   group_by(gender) |>   summarise(     mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE)   ) This kind of workflow can answer questions such as:

What is average income by gender?


What is total revenue by region?


How many observations belong to each category?


What is the average score across departments?

I also became more comfortable with R’s pipe operator:
The Native Pipe |> or The Magrittr Pipe %>%
which makes a sequence of analytical operations easier to read.
Gradually, my understanding of analysis developed into a workflow:
Import → Inspect → Clean → Transform → Group → Summarise → Analyse → Visualise → Communicate.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Data Visualisation Using ggplot2
One of the most enjoyable parts of the programme was data visualisation.
I learnt that visualisation is much more than making a report colourful. A good graph should have a purpose. It should reveal a trend, highlight a difference, expose a relationship, show a distribution, or make a statistical message easier to understand.





One of the major packages explored was ggplot2.
With ggplot2, I learnt the concept of constructing visualisations through layers.
A typical graph may begin with:
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = income))
and then have a geometry added:
geom_point()
The aes() function defines how variables are mapped to visual properties such as the x-axis, y-axis, colour, fill, size, or shape.
Different geom_*() functions allow the analyst to create different kinds of graphs.
geom_point() is useful for scatterplots.
geom_bar() displays counts of categorical observations.
geom_col() is useful when bar heights have already been calculated.
geom_line() is particularly valuable when examining trends across time or another ordered variable.
geom_histogram() helps reveal the distribution of continuous data.
geom_boxplot() provides information about distributions, median values, spread, and potential outliers.
geom_smooth() can be used to display a fitted relationship between variables.
I also learnt about facet_wrap() and facet_grid() for creating separate panels for different groups.
Functions such as labs() make it possible to add meaningful titles, subtitles, axis labels, and captions, while themes such as theme_minimal(), theme_classic() and theme_bw() help control the appearance of the final visualisation.
The broader concepts of aesthetics, geometry, scales, layers, coordinates, themes, legends, and faceting became much clearer to me during the training.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Data Visualisation Using Base R
Alongside ggplot2, I was also introduced to Base R graphics.
This provided another perspective on visualisation and demonstrated that R contains built-in graphical capabilities even without additional packages.
Some important functions included:
plot() hist() barplot() boxplot() pie()
For example:
hist(data$income)
can quickly display the distribution of income.
Similarly:
boxplot(data$income)
can provide information about the median, variability, and possible outliers.
Working with both Base R and ggplot2 helped me appreciate their different strengths.
Base R can be excellent for rapid exploratory work, while ggplot2 offers a more structured, layered, and highly customisable approach to creating publication-quality visualisations.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Data Merging and Joining
Another important component of the training was merging and joining datasets.
In real analytical work, information is frequently spread across multiple files.
One table might contain demographic information while another contains transactions. A third might contain geographical information.
To analyse them together, they must be joined correctly.
I learnt functions including:
left_join() right_join() inner_join() full_join()
A left_join() retains all observations from the first dataset and adds matching information from the second.
An inner_join() keeps only observations whose keys exist in both datasets.
A full_join() retains observations from both sides whether or not a match exists.
The training also highlighted the importance of understanding keys, identifiers, duplicates and matching variables.
This was an important lesson because a badly executed join can silently multiply observations and produce perfectly calculated statistics from completely incorrect data. Data analysis has a mischievous sense of humour that way.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Markdown and Reproducible Reporting
The training introduced me to Markdown, which later became very important for working with reproducible reports.
Markdown provides a simple syntax for structuring written content.
For example:
# Main Heading  ## Subheading  **Bold text**  *Italic text*
This allowed me to understand how analytical writing could be structured without depending entirely on traditional word-processing software.
From Markdown, the programme progressed into the wider concept of reproducible reporting.
This became one of the most important parts of the training for me.
In a conventional workflow, an analyst may analyse data in R, save graphs manually, copy tables into Word, type statistical values into paragraphs, and then have to repeat those processes whenever the underlying data change.
That creates several opportunities for inconsistency.
A graph may be updated while the accompanying paragraph still reports an old figure. A table may contain a newly calculated value while the executive summary contains yesterday’s number.
Reproducible reporting provides a better approach by connecting the data, analytical code, results, graphs, tables, interpretation, and final document.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
section: Quarto: From R Analysis to Professional Publishing
text:
Quarto: From R Analysis to Professional Publishing
Quarto was one of the most important and transformative topics I encountered during the programme.



quarto logo


Initially, I understood Quarto mainly as a way of producing reports. As the training progressed, however, I discovered that its capabilities extend far beyond traditional reporting.
Quarto provides an environment in which an analyst can combine R code, explanatory writing, statistical results, tables, visualisations, equations, citations, references, and conclusions within a single reproducible project.
A standard Quarto document normally uses the .qmd extension.
For example:
analysis.qmd
A Quarto document can contain three major building blocks:
YAML, which controls the document;
Markdown, which contains the written explanation;
and R code chunks, which perform the actual calculations and generate output.
A simple Quarto document can therefore contain something like:
--- title: "Statistical Analysis" author: "Aare" format: html ---  # Introduction  This report presents an analysis conducted in R.  ```{r} summary(mtcars) ```
When the document is rendered, the R code is executed and the results are inserted automatically into the finished publication.
This was a major shift in the way I thought about reporting.
Instead of:
Analyse → Copy → Paste → Edit → Repeat
Quarto makes a workflow such as this possible:
Data → R Code → Statistical Analysis → Graphs and Tables → Interpretation → Render → Finished Publication
Another useful concept was controlling what the reader sees.
For example:
#| echo: false
allows the R code to execute without displaying the code itself in the final publication.
This is useful when preparing analytical reports for readers who need the findings but do not necessarily need to see every line of programming behind them.

Publishing to Different Formats
Another major strength of Quarto is that a single source project can be published in several forms.
I learnt how Quarto can support outputs such as HTML reports, Microsoft Word documents, PDF reports, presentations, books, technical documentation, blogs, and complete websites.
This made me understand Quarto not simply as a document-writing tool but as a genuine publishing system for data professionals.
The same analytical work can therefore move from an R environment into something suitable for colleagues, researchers, managers, students, clients, or the general public.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
section: Creating and Publishing Websites with Quarto
text:
Creating and Publishing Websites with Quarto
Perhaps one of the most exciting discoveries was learning that Quarto can be used to create and publish a complete website.
This considerably expanded my understanding of what an analyst can achieve with R-related tools.
A Quarto website can contain several interconnected pages such as:
Home, About, Projects, Portfolio, Research, Publications, Blog, Resources, and Contact pages.
Each page can be written as a .qmd document.
A project-level file named:
_quarto.yml
can then control the overall structure of the website.
This file can define the website title, navigation menu, themes, page structure, links, search functionality and other publishing settings.
A typical project could therefore look like:
portfolio/ │ ├── _quarto.yml ├── index.qmd ├── about.qmd ├── projects.qmd └── contact.qmd
Quarto then connects those individual files into a complete website.
This was especially meaningful because the training did not end at theoretical knowledge.
I applied what I learnt by creating my own data portfolio website:

adept-data.github.io
Building my portfolio represented an important milestone in the programme.
It gave me an online platform where I can continue to showcase my development in R programming, statistics, data analysis, data visualisation, reproducible reporting, Quarto, and other areas of data science.
The experience showed me how several apparently separate skills can combine into one complete project.
The R projects provide the analytical substance.
Markdown provides the written content.
Quarto provides the website structure and publishing system.
Git tracks the development history.
GitHub stores the repository.
GitHub Pages makes the resulting website available online.
The complete journey can therefore be represented as:

Learn R → Analyse Data → Create Visualisations → Document the Analysis → Build with Quarto → Track with Git → Publish through GitHub → Share a Professional Portfolio

That was one of the most significant practical outcomes of the training.
I did not merely learn that Quarto can build websites. I built and published one myself.
For a data analyst, this is particularly valuable because the portfolio becomes more than a résumé. It becomes living evidence of practical ability.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Git and GitHub
The programme also introduced me to Git and GitHub, which completed another important part of the modern data-science workflow.



Github


Git is a version-control system that allows changes to project files to be tracked over time.
This provides a much better alternative to keeping multiple confusing copies of the same analysis with filenames such as:
analysis_final.R analysis_final2.R analysis_final_corrected.R analysis_final_corrected_latest.R analysis_REAL_FINAL.R
Git allows project development to be recorded systematically.
I became familiar with commands and concepts such as:
git init git status git add git commit git push git pull git clone
I also learnt about repositories, commits, branches, remote repositories, merging, and project history.
GitHub complements Git by providing an online platform where repositories can be stored, shared, reviewed, collaborated on, and published.
For me, its importance became even more obvious when it was connected to my Quarto portfolio website.
Git and GitHub therefore became more than tools for storing code.
They became part of a workflow for documenting, managing and publishing my professional work.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
A Training Built Around Practice
An important strength of my experience with GBG Analytics was the lab-based nature of the programme.
The training involved practical demonstrations, hands-on exercises, assignments, coding practice, troubleshooting, independent experimentation, and video resources that I could revisit whenever necessary.
This reinforced an important truth about programming:
you cannot become comfortable with code merely by watching somebody else write it.
You have to write it.
You have to break it.
You have to wonder why an error message has suddenly developed a personal grudge against you.
Then you have to investigate, correct the mistake, and try again.
That process gradually builds confidence.
The supporting videos were particularly valuable because they made it possible to revisit difficult areas, repeat demonstrations, and practise concepts at my own pace.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
section: What the Training Changed for Me
text:
What the Training Changed for Me
The greatest benefit of the programme was not simply learning more R functions.
It changed the way I understand the entire analytical process.
I now see data analysis as a connected sequence:
Define the question → Import the data → Inspect → Clean → Transform → Merge → Analyse → Visualise → Interpret → Document → Reproduce → Version-control → Publish → Communicate.
That wider perspective is important.
A data analyst is not simply someone who knows how to calculate a mean or run a model.
A strong analyst must understand the underlying data, select appropriate analytical methods, write understandable code, design meaningful visualisations, explain findings clearly, make the work reproducible, preserve its history, and communicate the final product to other people.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
My Experience with GBG Analytics
My training with GBG Analytics from 21 July to 7 October 2026 represented an important stage in my development as a statistician, programmer and data professional.
R became considerably easier for me.
Data manipulation became more systematic.
Data cleaning became more intentional.
Visualisation became more meaningful.
Markdown gave structure to analytical writing.
Reproducibility changed how I think about reporting.
Git and GitHub introduced disciplined project management and publishing.
And Quarto showed me how analytical work can move beyond an R session and become a professional report, presentation, publication, or complete website.
Most importantly, these skills produced something tangible.

I created and published my own portfolio at adept-data.github.io.
That transition—from learning R code to publishing my own analytical portfolio—is one of the strongest outcomes of the programme for me.

title: R training with GBGAnalyst
text:
Recommendation
For anyone seeking practical training in R programming, statistics, data analysis, data cleaning, dplyr, data visualisation, Base R graphics, ggplot2, data merging, Markdown, reproducible reporting, Quarto, Git, GitHub, portfolio development, and modern data-science workflows, I would encourage you to consider GBG Analytics.
Data science can initially look like a collection of disconnected tools.
R is here.
Statistics is there.
Git sits somewhere else.
Quarto appears from another corner.
Then someone mentions GitHub, packages, Markdown, joins, YAML, rendering, repositories and websites, and suddenly the learning journey begins to resemble a family meeting where everybody is talking at once.
Good training helps connect those pieces.
That was one of the most valuable things this programme did for me.
The training did not simply make R easier.
It helped me see how programming, statistics, visualisation, reproducibility, version control, and publishing belong to the same professional workflow.
From writing R code to creating graphs, from manipulating datasets to writing reproducible reports, and from learning Quarto to publishing my own portfolio website, the journey has been practical, challenging, and worthwhile.
Thank you, GBG Analytics, for making the learning process practical and meaningful.

From learning R to publishing my own data portfolio—the journey continues.
